osfacts — scoped, honest OS process & socket facts

Features·seedling·proposed·JUL 25, 2026

A standalone Rust tool — one versioned snapshot of processes and sockets, scoped to the ask and honest about what it couldn't read — with kolu and drishti as its first two consumers.

Contents

  • User stories
  • The contract
  • Why not an existing tool
  • Internals
    • The regression suite is scar tissue
  • How kolu and drishti adopt it

osfacts is a product of its own — its own repo, its own README, its own CI — not a kolu module. One static Rust binary that answers what does the OS say about these processes and their sockets, scoped to exactly what you asked, honest about what it could not read, in about ten milliseconds. kolu and drishti are its first two consumers, and the reason to build it is that the tool they need genuinely does not exist — see the comparison below.Status: proposed, deliberately future work; nothing here ships yet. Every measurement in this note comes from the #1982 candidate sweep — the note is where that week’s conclusions live on after the scratchpads that produced them are gone.

The creed, one line per word — also the repo README’s opening:

  • Scoped — cost tracks the ask (--roots walks a subtree), never the host.
  • Attributed — every snapshot carries the full pid→ppid table, so a grandchild listener walks back to its root.
  • Honest — what it could not read is reported, never silently dropped.
  • Versioned — schema version first; a mismatched consumer fails loudly instead of parsing a half-understood shape into zero rows.
  • Fast — ~10 ms per snapshot, because interactive callers poll at seconds scale. This budget is the requirement that explains every rejection in the comparison table.

User stories

Five flows, one contract — every story is the same verb with different facets, never a consumer-shaped flag or mode:

who wants to know runs comes back
kolu’s port sensor, every ~5 s which ports this terminal’s subtree listens on osfacts snapshot --roots 4242 --procs --ports pid table + listener rows with raw addresses; unreadable pids listed, so a blind terminal renders blind, not empty
drishti’s inspector the process tree under a service, with memory and age osfacts snapshot --roots 991 --procs --mem --start-time one row per descendant with RSS and start time
kolu’s daemon supervisor is this pid still mine, and since when osfacts snapshot --pids 991 --start-time a start time to compare against the recorded one
padi’s socket takeover which pids hold this unix socket osfacts socket-holders /run/user/1000/padi.sock the holder pids, or none
a human at any shell all of it, readable osfacts snapshot --json | jq the same facts as JSON

The contract

One verb, composable facets, first-class scoping.

osfacts snapshot --roots 4242,4310 --procs --ports
osfacts snapshot --pids 991 --mem --start-time
osfacts socket-holders /run/user/1000/padi.sock
  • Scoping is the headline. --roots walks the given pids’ subtrees, --pids takes an exact set, no flag means host-wide. Cost then tracks the ask, not the host — the property no surveyed tool has and the one the measurements say matters most.
  • Facets so a consumer pays only for what it reads: --procs, --ports, --mem, --start-time. socket-holders is a second verb because it answers a different question (a path, not a pid set).
  • One versioned schema. TSV on the hot path (V<TAB>1 first, tagged rows), --json for humans and one-offs.
  • Raw address bytes, never a wildcard boolean. Consumers keep exactly one classifier. Two predicates that must agree about ::ffff:0.0.0.0 is precisely how they come to disagree.
  • Cumulative CPU time per row, so CPU% is a consumer-side diff between two snapshots rather than a sampling delay inside the tool.This is why procs costs ~30 ms even at its lowest setting: it sleeps to compute a rate nobody asked it for. A one-shot sampler should never sleep.
  • A MANDATORY unreadable section. Every pid that could not be inspected is reported, with its errno — the policy of what is fatal stays in the consumer, the only layer that knows which pids it asked about.The sudo lesson made structural: when an unreadable pid was silently dropped, one sudo password prompt emptied the Ports section for every terminal on the host; when it threw indiscriminately, one foreign-uid descendant did the same.

Why not an existing tool

Every candidate was measured, not surveyed, and each fails on the contract above rather than on packaging — anything merely absent from nixpkgs could be packaged in an afternoon, so packaging never counts as a disqualifier.Earlier drafts listed “not packaged for darwin” against osquery and “not in nixpkgs” against portls. Both struck: a packaging gap is an errand, not an architecture verdict. The rows now stand on what each tool is. The repo README carries this same table:

candidate disqualifier
osquery the wrong operational model: a resident fleet-telemetry agent with a SQL surface, measured at ~378 ms per query and ~158 MB — built for querying thousands of machines every few minutes, not one machine every five seconds on a 10 ms budget
procs discards the bind address — loopback and wildcard collapse to one row
portls no PPID, no process table — a listener cannot be walked back to its root
rustnet interactive capture TUI, needs packet-capture privilege
portview listener rows only, no process table — a shell → npm → node server cannot be walked back to its terminal, because npm holds no listener and never appears. No subtree scoping either: its single-port query is a host-wide scan plus a filter (26.0 ms full vs 25.1 ms scoped)
sysinfo+listeners wrapping the two crates enumerates the process list twice: 23 ms darwin / ~100 ms linux against 10 ms for a single pass — and listeners shipped the v4-mapped decode bug we fixed upstream
lsof / netstat lsof measured 93 ms; macOS netstat is intermittently blind — success and zero rows in one sampling window, 29 rows in the next, same boot

portview is also the strongest evidence for building this: it measures 9.9 ms on darwin against our C helper’s 10.6 ms on the same box by the same method, in Rust, in a single pass. Single-pass Rust matches C — the language was never the constraint, the double enumeration was. That measurement is what settles osfacts on Rust.

Internals

One pass per platform, and no more:

  • linux — /proc, scoped by descending /proc/<pid>/task/<tid>/children from each root rather than reading the whole pid table. That descent is exactly the u-port-scan-subtree-descent opportunity, and the cost accounting says it is worth ~96% of a scoped pass.
  • darwin — a single libproc pass (proc_listpids → proc_pidinfo → proc_pidfdinfo), the shape the C helper already proved at ~4 ms of real work.

Crates only where earned. The fixed listeners for darwin address decoding once the upstream fix merges — and not sysinfo: pairing them walks the host twice, which is disqualified by construction.

The regression suite is scar tissue

Every one of these is a bug that actually happened, so the suite is written from the scars rather than from imagination — cargo integration tests, its own CI, both platforms:

  • the five bind fixtures (127.0.0.1, 0.0.0.0, ::1, ::, ::ffff:127.0.0.1);
  • v4-mapped vs v4-compatible — the upstream crate reported ::ffff:127.0.0.1 as ::127.0.0.1;
  • dual-stack flag ordering — insi_vflag sets BOTH bits for ::, so testing INI_IPV4 first narrows the wildcard to 0.0.0.0. Two independent tools and our own C helper each had this;
  • silent-empty detection — a mechanism that answers “no ports” successfully is the worst possible failure here, and macOS netstat does it intermittently;
  • the unreadable contract — an uninspectable pid must appear in output.

How kolu and drishti adopt it

Inside kolu the OS is inspected in five places today, each with its own hand-rolled reader, its own error policy, and its own platform split — five answers to one question, and every one a place a platform quirk can be got wrong independently.The week that produced #1982 found four such quirks, each fixed in exactly one of the five readers. All five collapse into calls to the one binary:

consumer today asks reads today
@kolu/port-scan a subtree’s processes + listening ports linux /proc; darwin a C libproc helper
memorySampler.ts per-pid RSS its own /proc / libproc path
socketHolder.ts which pids hold a unix socket path /proc/net/unix; darwin lsof
daemon supervisor process start time / uptime, “is this pid still ours” its own reads
drishti process inspection hand-rolled lsof

Migration order: darwin C helper → linux TS reader → memorySampler → socketHolder; drishti wholesale once the contract is stable. Each step is a consumer deleting its own OS traversal, and each is independently revertible.

Out of scope, deliberately: foreground process (a PTY-fd fact — tcgetpgrp on the pty, so it stays kaval’s), anything requiring root, and any daemon/resident mode. This is a one-shot sampler; if startup cost ever becomes the problem, the answer is to revisit the operational model, not to hide it behind a resident process. The same restraint applies outward: no TUI, no kill, no docker verbs — the broad user-facing surface is what made portls and portview wrong for embedding, and osfacts stays embeddable by staying narrow.
